exam.subject: Biology
exam.title: Eritrean Secondary Education Certificate Examinations 2018 – Biology

parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 60 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1.30 points. There is only one best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part II – Completion and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains fifteen work out and short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty two points.

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Biology textbooks Grades 9–12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not part of the Cell Theory?

options.A: All life is made of cells.
options.B: Cells are the smallest units of life.
options.D: All cells have mitochondria for energy production.

explanation_steps: The cell theory has three statements: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the smallest (basic) unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.
Mitochondria are not in the theory – and prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no mitochondria at all. Answer: D.
tips: Cell theory = made of cells + basic unit + from pre-existing cells.

similar_questions.stem: Which scientist's statement 'all cells come from pre-existing cells' completed the cell theory?
explanation_steps: Virchow (1855) added 'omnis cellula e cellula'. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Rods, spheres and spirals are shapes of cells observed in
explanation_steps: The three common shapes of bacterial cells are cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods) and spirilla (spirals). Answer: D.
tips: Coccus = sphere, bacillus = rod, spirillum = spiral.

similar_questions.stem: Rod-shaped bacteria are called
explanation_steps: Bacillus = rod. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Most organelles in a eukaryotic cell are found in the
explanation_steps: The cytoplasm is the jelly-like material between the cell membrane and the nucleus; mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi bodies, lysosomes, chloroplasts and vacuoles are suspended in it. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The site of most chemical reactions of the cell, containing the organelles, is the
explanation_steps: Cytoplasm. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the largest component of the circulatory system?
explanation_steps: Systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to all parts of the body and back to the right atrium.
Coronary (heart muscle), hepatic portal (gut → liver) and renal (kidney) circulations are parts of it; pulmonary circulation only serves the lungs. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: The circulation that carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs is
explanation_steps: Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Darwin's theory considers all of the following concepts except

options.B: use and disuse of an organ.

explanation_steps: Darwin's natural selection: overproduction, variation, struggle for existence, survival of the fittest.
Use and disuse (and inheritance of acquired characters) belongs to Lamarck's theory. Answer: B.
tips: Giraffe neck stretched by use = Lamarck; long-necked variants survive = Darwin.

similar_questions.stem: 'Inheritance of acquired characteristics' was proposed by
explanation_steps: Lamarck. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Theories of evolution – Lamarck and Darwin

questions.stem: The lowest level of environmental complexity that includes living and nonliving things is the
explanation_steps: Species, population and community contain only living things.
An ecosystem is a community plus its nonliving (abiotic) environment – the lowest level with both. Biome and biosphere are higher levels. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: All the populations of different species living in one area form a
explanation_steps: Populations of different species together = community. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following organs does not have any role in the excretory system?
explanation_steps: Excretory organs: kidneys (urine), lungs (CO₂ and water vapour), skin (sweat), liver (urea formation, bile pigments).
The heart pumps blood but excretes nothing. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which organ converts excess amino acids into urea?
explanation_steps: Deamination and urea formation occur in the liver. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which statement is incorrect about the organisms grouped under the kingdom Monera?

options.D: Some members of the kingdom are parasites.
options.E: Majority of the members possess cell wall made up of Chitin.

explanation_steps: Monerans are unicellular prokaryotes; some are photosynthetic (cyanobacteria) or chemosynthetic autotrophs, others heterotrophs including parasites.
Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan; chitin is the wall material of fungi. Answer: E.
tips: Chitin → fungi (and arthropod exoskeletons); cellulose → plants; peptidoglycan → bacteria.

similar_questions.stem: The cell walls of fungi are made mainly of
explanation_steps: Chitin. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following cellular activities is not a type of cell division?
explanation_steps: Binary fission, multiple fission, budding (unequal division, e.g. yeast) and mitosis all involve division of a cell.

Fragmentation is the breaking of a multicellular body/filament into pieces that grow into new individuals; the textbook contrasts it with cell division ('by simple cell division or fragmentation'). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Yeast cells multiply by unequal division of the cell called
explanation_steps: Yeast reproduces by budding. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Budding and multiple fission are forms of asexual reproduction rather than 'cell division' in the strict sense; E (fragmentation) is keyed because the textbook (p.66) contrasts fragmentation with cell division.

questions.stem: The organisms Euglena and Entamoeba belong to the kingdom
explanation_steps: Both are unicellular eukaryotes: Euglena (a flagellate with chloroplasts) and Entamoeba (an amoeba that causes amoebic dysentery) are protists. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, belongs to the kingdom
explanation_steps: Plasmodium is a sporozoan protist. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A balanced diet contains the following nutrients.

options.A: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals and water
options.B: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals and nucleic acids
options.C: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins and minerals
options.E: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids and minerals

explanation_steps: A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients in the right proportions: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals and water (plus roughage).
Nucleic acids are not a dietary requirement. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which nutrient is needed in the largest amount and makes up about two-thirds of body mass?
explanation_steps: Water. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following tissues is not a lymphatic tissue.
explanation_steps: Lymphatic tissue (lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils) is packed with white blood cells (leukocytes) – lymphocytes and macrophages.
Erythrocytes (red blood cells) belong to blood, not lymph; lymph lacks red blood cells. Answer: C.
tips: Lymph = blood plasma-like fluid without red cells and large proteins.

similar_questions.stem: Which component of blood is NOT normally found in lymph?
explanation_steps: Lymph contains most blood materials except red blood cells and large proteins. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: The options are cells, not tissues (wording of the paper); the intended meaning is 'cells not found in lymphatic tissue'.

questions.stem: The ______ makes the axon look like a necklace of sausage-shaped beads.

options.B: cell body of the nerve cell

explanation_steps: Textbook: longer axons are covered with a myelin sheath, a series of fatty cells wrapped around the axon; 'these make the axon look like a necklace of sausage-shaped beads'.
The Schwann's sheath is the outer covering that helps repair injured axons. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: The myelin sheath of a neuron works like
explanation_steps: It insulates the axon and speeds up impulses. Answer: B.

questions.stem: ______ are chemical messengers that are released from the axon terminals to cross the synaptic gap and reach the receptor sites of other neurons.
explanation_steps: At a synapse the impulse causes the axon terminal to release neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine) that diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors of the next neuron. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: The small gap between two neurons is the
explanation_steps: Synapse. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Smooth muscles form the walls of the following organs except the
explanation_steps: Smooth (involuntary, visceral) muscle lines hollow organs: stomach, intestine, bladder, uterus, blood vessels.
The wall of the heart is cardiac muscle. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which type of muscle is striated and under voluntary control?
explanation_steps: Skeletal muscle. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which part of a flowering plant grows continuously throughout the life of the plant?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The tips of the stem and roots continue to grow throughout the life of the plant' because of apical meristems.
Leaves have limited growth. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Tissues whose cells divide continuously to produce new cells are called
explanation_steps: Meristematic tissues. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The part of a seed embryo that develops into the shoot system is the
explanation_steps: In a germinating seed the radicle becomes the root and the plumule becomes the shoot. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The first structure to emerge from a germinating bean seed, which becomes the root, is the
explanation_steps: Radicle. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The type of gene mutation where a section of the DNA strand carrying one or more nucleotide pairs rotates through 180° is called
explanation_steps: Inversion: a segment is cut out, turned through 180° and re-inserted, reversing the base sequence. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: A mutation in which one base is replaced by another is
explanation_steps: Substitution. Answer: C.

questions.stem: For an organism with 48 chromosomes per cell, the number of chromosomes in each gamete is
explanation_steps: Gametes are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number (diploid 2n → haploid n).
48 ÷ 2 = 24. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. How many are in a human sperm cell?
explanation_steps: 46 ÷ 2 = 23. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents a heterozygous genotype for a given trait?
explanation_steps: Heterozygous = two different alleles of the same gene: Tt. TT, RR, tt are homozygous; T and R are letters for different genes. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: A plant with genotype tt is
explanation_steps: Two recessive alleles. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A cell under a microscope reveals cell walls and membrane-bounded organelles. This cell is most probably

options.B: either a plant or bacterial cell.
options.C: a plant, animal, or bacterial cell.

explanation_steps: Animal cells have no cell wall; bacteria have cell walls but no membrane-bound organelles.
Cell wall + membrane-bound organelles → a plant cell (among the options). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A cell has ribosomes and a cell wall but no nucleus. It is
explanation_steps: No nucleus = prokaryote. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which one of the following processes could result in the net movement of a substance into a cell, if the substance is more concentrated in the cell than in the surroundings?
explanation_steps: Moving a substance into a cell where it is already more concentrated means moving it against its concentration gradient.
Only active transport (using ATP and carrier proteins) does this. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which process needs energy from the cell?
explanation_steps: Active transport. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The three basic structures of all cells consist of the
explanation_steps: The textbook describes the basic parts of a cell as the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. Answer: A.
(Prokaryotes have genetic material but no true nucleus – the textbook's 'three basic structures' refers to the typical cell.)

similar_questions.stem: Which structure controls the activities of a eukaryotic cell?
explanation_steps: The nucleus contains DNA and controls the cell. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The function of the nose piece of a light microscope is to

options.B: slowly bring an image in focus.

explanation_steps: The revolving nose piece carries the objective lenses and is turned to bring the required objective into position.
Lenses magnify, the fine adjustment focuses slowly, the mirror/lamp illuminates, the stage clips hold the slide. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which part of the microscope is used to focus slowly at high power?
explanation_steps: Fine adjustment knob. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The types of antibodies produced in the plasma of a person with blood type O are
explanation_steps: Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
There is no 'anti-O'. Answer: D.
tips: Group O = universal donor (no antigens); AB = universal recipient (no antibodies).

similar_questions.stem: A person with blood group AB has which antibodies in the plasma?
explanation_steps: AB has both antigens, so neither antibody. Answer: D.

questions.stem: A piece of food dropped on your exercise book, and the paper changed its color and became translucent. This indicates that the food contains
explanation_steps: The grease-spot (translucent spot) test: fats and oils leave a translucent patch on paper that does not dry out. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which reagent turns blue-black with starch?
explanation_steps: Iodine test for starch. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about polysaccharides? They

options.C: can be found in both plants and animals.

explanation_steps: Polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen) are large, insoluble, non-sweet molecules; starch/cellulose in plants, glycogen in animals.
Sweetness is a property of mono- and disaccharides (sugars). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which carbohydrate is the storage polysaccharide of animals?
explanation_steps: Glycogen (liver and muscle). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows the correct pathway of blood flow in the circulatory system?

options.A: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery
options.B: Right atrium → left atrium → pulmonary artery

explanation_steps: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and is pumped into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Answer: A.
Atria do not connect directly; the left ventricle pumps into the aorta, not the pulmonary artery.

similar_questions.stem: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the heart through the
explanation_steps: Pulmonary veins → left atrium. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The main metabolic wastes produced during cellular respiration in most mammals are
explanation_steps: Aerobic respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy.
CO₂ and water are the waste products of respiration (urea comes from protein breakdown, bile pigments from haemoglobin). Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Urea is formed from the breakdown of
explanation_steps: Deamination of excess amino acids in the liver. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: The following conditions are results of abnormal secretion of the pituitary gland except
explanation_steps: Growth hormone excess → gigantism (childhood) or acromegaly (adult); deficiency → dwarfism; lack of ADH (posterior pituitary) → diabetes insipidus.
Goitre is an enlargement of the thyroid gland (iodine deficiency). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Enlargement of the thyroid gland due to iodine deficiency is called
explanation_steps: Goitre. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Calcium level in the blood is regulated by the
explanation_steps: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium; calcitonin from the thyroid gland lowers it. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone lowers blood calcium level?
explanation_steps: Calcitonin (thyroid). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about endoskeleton?

options.A: Comprises of cartilage, ligaments and bones.
options.C: Can support size and weight of the body.

explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.1 (endoskeleton vs exoskeleton): the endoskeleton 'grows fairly smoothly and evenly, no moulting' and 'being internal, can support great size and weight'. Moulting (D) belongs to the exoskeleton.
B is the exact table statement and is keyed. Answer: B.

However C (support size and weight – from the same table), A (the human skeletal system comprises cartilages, ligaments and bones, p.53) and E (bones store minerals and fat, p.54) are also true statements.
tips: Exoskeleton must be moulted; endoskeleton grows with the body.

similar_questions.stem: Which feature belongs to an exoskeleton but not to an endoskeleton?

options.C: Must be moulted to allow growth

explanation_steps: An exoskeleton cannot grow and must be shed. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Several options are true: B and C come from textbook Table 3.1, A and E are true of the (human) skeleton. Only D is false. B keyed, C also accepted; a teacher must decide how to mark A and E.

questions.stem: A bone is composed of
explanation_steps: Textbook: bone develops from cartilage (key players are cartilage cells and bone cells); compact bone is filled with blood vessels and rich in nerves; bone marrow makes blood cells; bone tissue stores fats and minerals (calcium, phosphorus).
Each option names something found in bone, so the intended answer is E.

similar_questions.stem: Red blood cells are produced in the
explanation_steps: Red marrow in spongy bone. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Loosely worded: 'fatty minerals' is not a real term and mature bone contains bone cells rather than cartilage cells. E is keyed because each option paraphrases a component mentioned on textbook pp.54-55.

questions.stem: Which of the following systems has little to contribute to the homeostasis of an organism?
explanation_steps: Homeostasis (constant internal environment) is maintained by the nervous and endocrine systems (control) and the excretory and respiratory systems (removing wastes, water/salt and CO₂ balance).
The reproductive system serves the survival of the species, not the internal balance of the individual. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which organ plays the main role in regulating the water content of the blood?
explanation_steps: Osmoregulation by the kidneys. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following statements is true about Neo Darwinism.

options.A: It rejects the Theory of Natural Selection.
options.B: It accepted the theory of 'Use and Disuse of organs'.
options.D: It uses mutation to explain the source of variation.
options.E: It has no information about DNA as a genetic material.

explanation_steps: Neo-Darwinism (modern synthesis) keeps natural selection and adds genetics: variation comes from mutation and genetic recombination, inherited through genes/DNA.
It rejects Lamarck's use and disuse. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: According to Neo-Darwinism, the raw material for evolution is provided by
explanation_steps: Mutation and recombination create variation. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes is not involved in the Carbon Cycle?
explanation_steps: Carbon moves by photosynthesis (CO₂ → organic compounds), respiration and decomposition (back to CO₂), and combustion.
Evaporation is part of the water cycle. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
explanation_steps: Photosynthesis. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The type of vegetation in a given biome is not greatly influenced by

options.A: the type of organisms that inhabit it.

explanation_steps: Biomes are defined by climate (temperature and rainfall) and soil, which determine the dominant vegetation.
The animals living there depend on the vegetation rather than determining it. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A biome with very low rainfall and plants with spines and water-storing stems is a
explanation_steps: Desert. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The name 'Red Sea' is very much associated with
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The Red Sea periodically becomes red when the species [of cyanobacteria] bearing red pigment is abundant.' Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Cyanobacteria are important in the soil because they can
explanation_steps: Many cyanobacteria fix nitrogen into nitrates/ammonia. Answer: A.

questions.stem: The figure shows part of an unbranched filament of cylindrical cells, each containing a ribbon-like chloroplast coiled in a spiral and a central nucleus. The organism indicated in the figure is
questions.image_alt: Drawing of part of an unbranched filament made of long cylindrical cells; inside each cell a ribbon-shaped chloroplast winds in a spiral (helix) along the cell wall, with a dark nucleus in the centre.
explanation_steps: A filament of cylindrical cells each containing a spiral (helical) ribbon-shaped chloroplast is the green alga Spirogyra. Answer: B.
Paramecium and amoeba are single cells without chloroplasts; Chlamydomonas is a single biflagellate cell with a cup-shaped chloroplast; Volvox is a spherical colony.

similar_questions.stem: A unicellular green alga with two flagella, a cup-shaped chloroplast and a red eyespot is
explanation_steps: Chlamydomonas. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The figure shows part of an unbranched filament of cylindrical cells, each containing a ribbon-like chloroplast coiled in a spiral and a central nucleus. The organism indicated in the figure reproduces by
questions.image_alt: Drawing of part of an unbranched filament made of long cylindrical cells; inside each cell a ribbon-shaped chloroplast winds in a spiral (helix) along the cell wall, with a dark nucleus in the centre.
explanation_steps: The organism is Spirogyra. Textbook: 'Spirogyra reproduces in two ways. The first method is by simple cell division known as fission. During unfavourable conditions Spirogyra reproduce by a process known as conjugation' (Fig. 2.11 shows conjugation).
Conjugation, the method characteristic of Spirogyra and shown in the textbook figure, is keyed. Answer: B.
Binary fission (C) is also named in the textbook, and fragmentation (A) of filaments is the usual asexual method in other books.
tips: Spirogyra: conjugation (sexual) when conditions are bad.

similar_questions.stem: During conjugation in Spirogyra, the contents of one cell

options.B: pass through a conjugation canal and fuse with the contents of another cell

explanation_steps: A conjugation tube joins cells of two filaments and the contents fuse to form a zygospore. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Two options fit the textbook (p.74): fission (C) and conjugation (B); fragmentation (A) is also a real method of Spirogyra. B keyed, C accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: How does a succulent plant adapt to its environment?

options.A: By modifying the leaves to spines to reduce loss of water by transpiration.
options.B: The stem takes over the process of photosynthesis.
options.C: By modifying the stem to store water.
options.D: Its leaves possess few stomata covered with wax in order to reduce water loss.

explanation_steps: Succulents (e.g. cactus, Euphorbia) of dry areas: leaves reduced to spines, green stem photosynthesises, fleshy stem stores water, few sunken/waxy stomata.
All options are adaptations. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Plants adapted to live in very dry conditions are called
explanation_steps: Xerophytes. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.2 Adaptations of plants to water – xerophytes/succulents

questions.stem: Animals adapt to low temperature by

options.A: having large ears that provide a large surface area.
options.B: hormonal changes that increase metabolic rate.
options.C: absence of fat layer under the skin.

explanation_steps: Textbook list for low temperatures: hormonal changes that boost metabolic rate, good appetite, shivering, insulation (fur, fat), hibernation, basking, small body projections.
Large ears, no fat, nocturnal habits and aestivation are adaptations to heat. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Why does the Arctic fox have small ears?
explanation_steps: Small projections reduce the surface area for heat loss. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.3.1 Adaptations of animals to low temperatures

questions.stem: The disease called atherosclerosis is caused by

options.A: deposition of highly saturated fats in the walls of the blood vessels.
options.B: severe protein inadequacy in the diet.
options.C: lack of vitamins in the diet.

explanation_steps: Atherosclerosis: fatty deposits (cholesterol, saturated fats) build up in artery walls, narrowing them and raising the risk of heart attack and stroke. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Severe protein deficiency in young children causes
explanation_steps: Kwashiorkor. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The passage of partially digested food from the stomach to the small intestine is controlled by
explanation_steps: The pyloric sphincter at the lower end of the stomach relaxes to release chyme into the duodenum a little at a time. Answer: B.
The cardiac sphincter is at the upper end (oesophagus → stomach).

similar_questions.stem: The ring of muscle between the oesophagus and the stomach is the
explanation_steps: Cardiac sphincter. Answer: B.

questions.stem: External respiration in humans

options.C: is the process of oxidation of glucose or fat molecules.
options.D: is the process of inhaling carbon dioxide and exhaling oxygen.

explanation_steps: External respiration = exchange of gases between the air in the alveoli and the blood – in the lungs. Answer: B.
Internal (cellular) respiration occurs in body cells and oxidises glucose; we inhale O₂, not CO₂.

similar_questions.stem: The exchange of gases between blood and body tissues is called
explanation_steps: Internal respiration. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which statement is incorrect about the cerebrum?

options.A: It makes up about 80% of the total brain mass.
options.B: It plays an important role in memory.
options.C: The right hemisphere controls the left side of the body.
options.D: Each cerebral hemisphere is divided into lobes.

explanation_steps: Textbook: the cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, about 80 % of the total brain mass, divided into left and right hemispheres, each divided into lobes; it is the centre of memory, thought and voluntary action; each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body.
All four statements are correct, so none is incorrect. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and muscular movement?
explanation_steps: Cerebellum. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The luteinizing hormone (LH), that stimulates the production of testosterone and progesterone, is secreted by the
explanation_steps: LH is a gonadotrophin made by the anterior pituitary gland; it acts on the testes (testosterone) and ovaries (ovulation, corpus luteum → progesterone). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which pituitary hormone stimulates the growth of follicles in the ovary?
explanation_steps: Follicle-stimulating hormone. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Dormant seeds

options.B: are subject to internal and external factors.
options.C: enable plants to avoid periods of environmental stress.
options.D: ensure the survival of the species.

explanation_steps: Dormancy: a living (viable) seed stays inactive until conditions are suitable; it is controlled by internal factors (hormones like abscisic acid, immature embryo, hard seed coat) and external factors (water, temperature, light).
It lets the plant survive unfavourable seasons and so ensures survival of the species. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which plant hormone promotes seed dormancy?
explanation_steps: Abscisic acid. Answer: C.

questions.stem: A messenger RNA is synthesized from a ______ template.
explanation_steps: Transcription: one strand of DNA is used as the template to make a complementary mRNA in the nucleus. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: If a DNA template strand reads TAC, the mRNA codon is
explanation_steps: Complement of T-A-C with U for T: A-U-G. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which sub-units of a nucleotide are referred to as 'the steps of the DNA ladder'?
explanation_steps: DNA is like a twisted ladder: the sides are alternating deoxyribose sugar and phosphate; the steps (rungs) are paired nitrogenous bases (A–T, G–C). Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: In DNA, adenine always pairs with
explanation_steps: A pairs with T. Answer: C.

questions.stem: 'Sewa' (our local alcoholic drink) is produced by a process called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The process of anaerobic respiration in some bacteria and yeast is called fermentation … Yeasts are used for … alcoholic beverages such as wine, beer, mies or suwa … This process is called alcohol fermentation.'
So sewa is made by alcoholic fermentation, which is a form of anaerobic respiration. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The products of alcoholic fermentation are
explanation_steps: Glucose → ethanol + CO₂ + 2 ATP. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Evolutionary evidence of paleontology depends on
explanation_steps: Palaeontology is the study of fossils; fossils form and are preserved in layers of sedimentary rock, whose order shows their relative age. Answer: B.
Embryos, biochemistry and homologous organs are other lines of evidence.

similar_questions.stem: In undisturbed sedimentary rocks, the oldest fossils are found in the
explanation_steps: Lower layers were deposited first. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Antigens are

options.A: macromolecules that induce the response of the immune system.
options.B: proteins produced by white blood cells.
options.C: physical components of the immune system.
options.D: proteins that help the body to resist infections.
options.E: macromolecules that can easily be eliminated by the physical barriers.

explanation_steps: An antigen is a foreign macromolecule (protein, polysaccharide) that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies. Answer: A.
B and D describe antibodies.

similar_questions.stem: Proteins produced by lymphocytes that bind specific antigens are
explanation_steps: Antibodies. Answer: B.

questions.stem: If you drink too much water within a short period of time, the result will be

options.E: increased secretion of both oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone.

explanation_steps: Excess water lowers the solute concentration of the blood; the hypothalamus detects this and the pituitary releases LESS ADH.
Less ADH → collecting ducts less permeable → large volumes of dilute urine. Oxytocin is unrelated. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: On a hot day with heavy sweating, ADH secretion
explanation_steps: Water loss → more ADH → more water reabsorbed → concentrated urine. Answer: B.

questions.stem: After an accident, Dawit cannot move his neck to any direction. This is because he was injured in his
explanation_steps: Turning the head is made possible by the pivot joint between the atlas and axis vertebrae. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The knee and elbow are examples of
explanation_steps: Hinge joints. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Neck movement also involves the gliding joints between vertebrae; 'pivot joint' is the intended answer (rotation of the head).

questions.stem: Which of the following elaborate beneficial economic importance of fungi?

options.A: Fungi do not cause diseases to plants.
options.B: Various strains of yeast are used to make beer, wine and bread.
options.C: Some species of fungi are used to produce the antibiotics penicillin.
options.D: Some fungi are pathogenic and affect humans adversely.

explanation_steps: Beneficial: yeasts in brewing and baking (B); Penicillium gives penicillin (C). A is false (many fungi cause plant diseases) and D is harmful importance. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which fungus is used in making bread?
explanation_steps: Yeast (Saccharomyces). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Sea otters live in the ocean. Which of the following is not likely to be a limiting factor on the sea otter population?
explanation_steps: Limiting factors of a population include competition, predation, disease, food supply and migration.
Drought (lack of rain) cannot affect a population living in the ocean. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a density-dependent limiting factor?
explanation_steps: Disease spreads faster in dense populations. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.note: Population growth and limiting factors; exact page approximate.

questions.stem: Which plant hormone will you recommend to a farmer who wants to grow a plant which is taller than it usually grows?
explanation_steps: Gibberellins cause marked stem elongation (e.g. dwarf plants treated with gibberellin grow tall). Answer: E.
Ethylene ripens fruit, cytokinins promote cell division, abscisic acid causes dormancy.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone speeds up the ripening of fruits?
explanation_steps: Ethylene. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An umbilical cord is

options.A: a long cord-like structure attached to the body of the embryo.
options.B: supplied with veins of oxygenated blood and food from placenta.
options.C: supplied with arteries of deoxygenated blood from the embryo.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The placenta is connected to the body of the embryo by a long, cord-like structure called the umbilical cord. The cord is supplied with arteries and veins. The vein transports food and oxygenated blood from the placenta to the embryo, while the artery transports waste … and deoxygenated blood from the embryo to the placenta.'
A, B and C are all correct. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which substance passes from the fetus to the mother through the placenta?
explanation_steps: Wastes (urea, CO₂) go from fetus to mother. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The blood group of different couples is listed in the table. From which of the following couples can a child be born with blood group AB? (I: man homozygous for group A, woman homozygous for group B; II: man homozygous for group B, woman homozygous for group A; III: man homozygous for group A, woman with group AB; IV: man with group AB, woman homozygous for group B)
explanation_steps: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant; a child is AB when it receives Iᴬ from one parent and Iᴮ from the other.
I and II: IᴬIᴬ × IᴮIᴮ → all children IᴬIᴮ (AB).
III: IᴬIᴬ × IᴬIᴮ → ½ IᴬIᴬ (A), ½ IᴬIᴮ (AB).
IV: IᴬIᴮ × IᴮIᴮ → ½ IᴬIᴮ (AB), ½ IᴮIᴮ (B).
Every couple can have an AB child. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Parents with genotypes Iᴬi and Iᴮi can have children of which blood groups?
explanation_steps: Punnett square: IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O). Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4 Codominance and multiple alleles – ABO blood groups

questions.stem: State two common characteristics of living things. (1 point)
questions.answer: Any two: living things are made of cells; they grow and develop; they reproduce; they respond to stimuli (irritability); they obtain and use energy – respiration/metabolism; they excrete wastes; they move; they maintain homeostasis.
explanation_steps: List properties shared by all organisms and absent from non-living matter.
Any two correct characteristics, ½ point each.
marking_points: ½ point for each of two correct characteristics
tips: Mnemonic MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition.

similar_questions.stem: Viruses are often said to be 'on the border of life'. Give one characteristic of living things that viruses show and one they lack.
similar_questions.answer: Show: they reproduce (inside host cells) and contain nucleic acid (can mutate). Lack: cellular structure/metabolism – they cannot respire or grow outside a host cell.
explanation_steps: Compare virus properties with the characteristics of life (textbook G9 p.41).

questions.stem: ______ are connective tissues that hold one bone to another in the body, forming a joint. (0.5 point)
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Ligaments are the strong bands of connective tissue that bind bones to one another.' (Tendons attach muscles to bones.)

similar_questions.stem: Tough inelastic cords that attach muscles to bones are called ______.
explanation_steps: Tendons connect muscle to bone (G11 p.54).

questions.stem: There are two types of cell divisions in the human body. The formation of somatic cells of the body occurs by ___3.1___ cell division, whereas the formation of sex cells occurs by ___3.2___ cell division. (1 point)

subparts.question: Somatic cells are formed by ___ cell division.
Sex cells are formed by ___ cell division.

explanation_steps: Body (somatic) cells are produced by mitosis, which gives two diploid, genetically identical cells.
Sex cells (gametes) are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number (haploid).

similar_questions.stem: How many daughter cells are formed from one cell by (a) mitosis, (b) meiosis?
explanation_steps: Mitosis: one division; meiosis: two successive divisions.

questions.stem: Define hydrophytes. (1 point)
questions.answer: Hydrophytes are plants that live in water or in very wet (water-logged) conditions – submerged, floating or in swamps (e.g. water lily, water hyacinth).
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Hydrophytes are plants that live in excessive water conditions…'; compare with xerophytes (dry) and mesophytes (moderate water).
marking_points: Plants that live in water / excessively wet conditions (1)

similar_questions.stem: Give two adaptations of hydrophytes to their environment.
similar_questions.answer: Any two: air spaces (aerenchyma) for buoyancy and gas exchange; stomata on the upper surface of floating leaves; reduced xylem and roots; thin or no cuticle; finely divided submerged leaves.
explanation_steps: Link each feature to plenty of water / lack of oxygen.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.2 Adaptations of plants to water – hydrophytes

questions.stem:
Complete the following questions. (1 point)
5.1 The elements that make up carbohydrates exist in a ratio of ______.
5.2 Write the general chemical formula of monosaccharides. ______
questions.answer: 5.1 C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1 (hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1, as in water). 5.2 (CH₂O)ₙ, i.e. CₙH₂ₙOₙ (e.g. C₆H₁₂O₆).

subparts.question: Ratio of the elements in carbohydrates
steps: As in water, two H for every O.

explanation_steps: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with H : O = 2 : 1.
Simple sugars have the empirical formula CH₂O; the general formula is (CH₂O)ₙ with n = 3–7, e.g. glucose C₆H₁₂O₆.

similar_questions.stem: Give the molecular formula of a pentose (5-carbon) monosaccharide such as ribose.
explanation_steps: n = 5 in (CH₂O)ₙ.

questions.stem: Generally there are two different types of reproduction: sexual and asexual. Define 6.1 sexual reproduction and 6.2 asexual reproduction. (1 point)
questions.answer:
6.1 Sexual reproduction is the production of offspring by the fusion of male and female gametes (fertilisation), usually from two parents; offspring show variation.
6.2 Asexual reproduction is the production of offspring from a single parent without the formation and fusion of gametes (by mitosis – fission, budding, fragmentation, vegetative propagation); offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

subparts.question: Sexual reproduction
subparts.answer: Offspring formed by fusion of male and female gametes.

subparts.question: Asexual reproduction
subparts.answer: Offspring formed from one parent without gametes.

explanation_steps: Key difference: gametes and fertilisation (sexual) versus one parent, no gametes (asexual).

similar_questions.stem: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of asexual reproduction.
similar_questions.answer: Advantage: rapid, needs only one parent, good traits kept. Disadvantage: no variation, so the population may not survive environmental change or disease.
explanation_steps: Think about speed versus genetic variation.

questions.stem:
Choose from the words in brackets to complete the information in the table. (3 points)
Blood vessels | Thickness of the walls (thick, thin and very thin) | Do they contain valves? (yes / no)
Arteries | 7.1 | 7.2
Veins | 7.3 | 7.4
Capillaries | 7.5 | 7.6

stem_tables.title: Question 7 table
columns: Thickness of the walls (thick, thin, very thin)

questions.answer: 7.1 thick; 7.2 no; 7.3 thin; 7.4 yes; 7.5 very thin; 7.6 no.
explanation_steps: Arteries carry blood at high pressure from the heart: thick, muscular, elastic walls; no valves along their length (only the semilunar valves at the exits of the heart).
Veins carry blood at low pressure: thinner walls, with valves to prevent backflow.
Capillaries: walls only one cell thick (very thin) for exchange; no valves.
marking_points: ½ point for each of the six boxes
tips: Pressure explains it: high pressure → thick wall; low pressure → valves needed.

similar_questions.stem: Why do veins, but not arteries, need valves?
similar_questions.answer: Blood in veins is under low pressure and could flow backwards (especially in the legs against gravity); valves allow flow only towards the heart. Arterial blood is pushed forward by the high pressure of each heartbeat.
explanation_steps: Relate valves to blood pressure.

questions.stem: Name the parts labeled 8.1–8.4 in the diagram of the human urinary system. (2 points) (8.1 points to one of the two bean-shaped organs at the back of the abdomen; 8.2 to the tube running down from it; 8.3 to the muscular bag in the pelvis; 8.4 to the tube leaving the bottom of the bag.)
questions.image_alt: Outline of the human trunk with ribs; two dark bean-shaped kidneys at the back with blood vessels; label 8.1 points to a kidney, 8.2 to the thin tube (ureter) running down, 8.3 to the dark bladder at the bottom, 8.4 to the short tube below the bladder.
explanation_steps: The kidneys filter blood and form urine; each ureter carries urine to the urinary bladder, which stores it; the urethra carries urine out of the body.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct label
tips: Order of urine flow: kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra (ureter comes before urethra alphabetically too).

similar_questions.stem: Which blood vessel brings blood to the kidney for filtration?
similar_questions.answer: The renal artery (blood leaves by the renal vein).
explanation_steps: Renal = kidney.

questions.stem:
Write the appropriate word (enzyme/hormone) that corresponds to the characteristics given below. (2 points)
9.1 Secretions of endocrine glands
9.2 Transported by blood
9.3 Chemically always proteins
9.4 Secretion of exocrine glands
explanation_steps: Endocrine (ductless) glands secrete hormones directly into the blood, which carries them to target organs (9.1, 9.2).
All enzymes are proteins; hormones may be proteins, amines or steroids (9.3).
Exocrine glands secrete juices that usually contain enzymes through ducts (textbook G11 p.1) (9.4).
marking_points: ½ point for each correct word

similar_questions.stem: Name one hormone that is a steroid and one that is a protein.
explanation_steps: Hormones are chemically diverse.

questions.stem: The heart pumps blood to flow through the blood vessels. How does lymph flow through the lymphatic vessels? (0.5 point)
questions.answer: By muscular activity: contraction of the skeletal muscles (and breathing movements) squeezes the lymphatic vessels and pushes lymph along, while valves in the vessels prevent backflow.
explanation_steps: The lymphatic system has no pump. Textbook: 'muscular activity largely influences the movement of lymph through the lymphatic vessels.'
marking_points: Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezing the vessels (valves prevent backflow) (0.5)

similar_questions.stem: Why can prolonged sitting without moving cause swelling of the feet?
similar_questions.answer: Leg muscles are inactive, so lymph (and venous blood) is not squeezed upwards; tissue fluid collects in the feet.
explanation_steps: Link to muscle pumping.

questions.stem: The figure shows a cross section of a dicot stem (with the pith in the centre and a ring of vascular bundles). Label the figure (11.1–11.5) with the appropriate word/phrase given below: Cortex, Epidermis, Xylem, Apex, Phloem, Midrib, Cambium. (2.5 points)
questions.image_alt: Circular cross section of a stem with 'Pith' in the centre and eight oval vascular bundles in a ring, each crossed by a thin white line. Label 11.1 points to the outer edge; 11.2 to the tissue between the bundles and the edge; 11.3 to the inner halves of two bundles; 11.4 to the white line in a bundle; 11.5 to the outer part of a lower bundle.
questions.answer: 11.1 epidermis; 11.2 cortex; 11.3 xylem; 11.4 cambium; 11.5 phloem. (Apex and midrib are distractors.)
explanation_steps: 11.1 points to the outermost boundary layer → epidermis.
11.2 points to the region between the epidermis and the vascular bundles → cortex.
In each vascular bundle of a dicot stem the xylem is on the inner side (towards the pith), the phloem on the outer side, and the cambium is the thin band between them.
11.3 arrows point to the inner part of the bundles → xylem; 11.4 points to the thin line across the bundle → cambium; 11.5 points to the outer part of a bundle → phloem.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct label
tips: Dicot stem from outside: epidermis → cortex → phloem → cambium → xylem → pith.

similar_questions.stem: How does the arrangement of vascular bundles differ between a dicot stem and a monocot stem?
similar_questions.answer: Dicot stem: bundles arranged in a ring, with cambium. Monocot stem: bundles scattered through the ground tissue, no cambium.
explanation_steps: Compare cross sections.

questions.review_flag: The scanned figure is small and the pointer lines for 11.3–11.5 are hard to read; the labels were assigned from the pointer positions (inner part of bundle = xylem, crossing line = cambium, outer part = phloem). A teacher should confirm on a clean copy.

questions.stem: An interaction between different species is known as ______. (0.5 point)
questions.answer: Inter-specific relation (inter-specific interaction), e.g. predation, parasitism, competition, symbiosis.
explanation_steps: Textbook G12 p.89: 'Inter-specific relations are interactions between different species'; interactions within one species are intra-specific.
marking_points: Inter-specific relation/interaction (0.5); accept symbiosis only if the teacher allows the broader term
tips: inter- = between (different species); intra- = within (same species).

similar_questions.stem: Competition between two lions for the same territory is an example of ______ competition.
explanation_steps: Same species → intra-specific.

questions.stem: List any two conditions that should be controlled in our body, to be maintained at particular levels during homeostasis. (1 point)
questions.answer: Any two: body temperature; blood glucose (sugar) level; water content / osmotic concentration of the blood; salt (ion) balance; pH of the blood; carbon dioxide/oxygen level; blood pressure.
explanation_steps: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment constant; the textbook's examples include temperature, blood sugar, water and salt balance.
marking_points: ½ point for each of two correct conditions

similar_questions.stem: Which hormones regulate the blood glucose level?
similar_questions.answer: Insulin (lowers it) and glucagon (raises it), both from the pancreas.
explanation_steps: Negative feedback by the islets of Langerhans.

questions.stem:
The figures A and B show the mechanism of breathing in humans (A: ribs and sternum returned to original position; B: ribs and sternum raised). (2 points)
14.1 Which figure shows inhalation?
14.2 Which figure shows exhalation?
14.3 Which figure shows relaxation of the diaphragm and decrease of the thorax volume?
14.4 Which figure shows contraction of the diaphragm and an increase of the thorax volume?
questions.image_alt: Two side views of the human chest. A: labelled 'Ribs and sternum returned to original position', diaphragm dome-shaped. B: labelled 'Ribs and sternum raised' and 'Rib cage', diaphragm flatter and chest larger.
explanation_steps: Inhalation: the diaphragm contracts (flattens, pulls down) and the intercostal muscles pull the ribs and sternum upward and outward → thorax volume increases, pressure falls, air enters. Figure B shows ribs raised.
Exhalation: the diaphragm relaxes (domes up) and the ribs and sternum return → thorax volume decreases, air is forced out. Figure A.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct letter

similar_questions.stem: During inhalation, what happens to the air pressure inside the lungs compared with atmospheric pressure?
similar_questions.answer: It becomes lower than atmospheric pressure, so air flows in.
explanation_steps: Volume up → pressure down (Boyle's law).

questions.stem:
Match body parts in Column A with explanation/functions in Column B. (3 points)
Column A: 15.1 Muscle; 15.2 Spinal cord; 15.3 Skull; 15.4 Appendicular skeleton; 15.5 Brain; 15.6 Heart.
Column B: A. Produces responses through reflex mechanisms; B. Limbs and girdles; C. Housed within the cranium; D. A pump; E. Produces the force responsible for movement; F. Comprises of the cranial, facial and 3 small bones of ear.

stem_tables.title: Column A / Column B
rows: A. Produces responses through reflex mechanisms
E. Produces the force responsible for movement
F. Comprises of the cranial, facial and 3 small bones of ear

explanation_steps: Muscles contract and produce the force for movement (E).
The spinal cord is the centre of reflex actions (A).
The skull consists of the cranial bones, facial bones and the three ear ossicles (F).
The appendicular skeleton = bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles (B).
The brain is housed within the cranium (C). The heart is a muscular pump (D).
marking_points: ½ point for each correct match (6 × ½)

similar_questions.stem: Name the two parts of the axial skeleton other than the skull.
similar_questions.answer: The vertebral column and the rib cage (ribs and sternum).
explanation_steps: Axial = skull + vertebral column + rib cage.
